content: Late congenital syphilis is a form of congenital syphilis that manifests in children aged 2 years or older who acquired the infection through transplacental transmission from their mother during pregnancy. One of the characteristic symptoms is the presence of blunted or notched upper incisor teeth, which are referred to as Hutchinson's teeth. Another common manifestation is inflammation of the cornea, medically termed interstitial keratitis, which can lead to visual impairment. Hearing loss may also occur due to damage to the auditory nerve, resulting in deafness. Affected individuals may exhibit frontal bossing, which is an abnormal prominence of the brow ridge. The nasal structure can be compromised, leading to a condition known as saddle nose, where the bony part of the nose collapses. Defects in the hard palate may also be observed. Joint abnormalities, such as swollen knees, are another potential symptom. The tibia may develop an abnormal shape, described as saber shins due to its bowing appearance. Facial bone structure can also be affected, with a shortened upper jaw (short maxillae) and a protruding lower jaw (protruding mandible) being notable features. A specific triad of symptoms, known as Hutchinson's triad, is frequently observed in cases of late congenital syphilis. This triad includes Hutchinson's teeth, interstitial keratitis, and deafness, and it is present in approximately 63% of affected individuals. Timely treatment with penicillin, administered before the onset of late-stage symptoms, is critical to prevent the development of these severe complications.
